message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties**

| Property | Value (standard conditions) | Notes |
|----------|-----------------------------|-------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average) | Dominated by the most abundant isotope, ^1H. |
| **Isotopes** | ^1H (protium, 99.98 %), ^2H (deuterium, 0.02 %), ^3H (tritium, trace, radioactive) | Deuterium and tritium are used in nuclear fusion research. |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ | One valence electron → highly reactive. |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | Highest among all elements. |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) | Highest of all elements. |
| **Electron affinity** | –0.754 eV (–72.8 kJ mol⁻¹) | Negative value indicates energy release when an electron is added. |
| **Molecular form** | H₂ (diatomic) | Most stable form at ambient conditions. |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) | Extremely low; requires cryogenic temperatures. |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) | Liquid hydrogen exists only under high pressure or low temperature. |
| **Density (gas, 0 °C, 1 atm)** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ | About 14.5 % of air’s density. |
| **Density (liquid, 20 K)** | 0.0708 g cm⁻³ | Lower than water; expands upon freezing. |
| **Specific heat (gas, 25 °C)** | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ | High due to light mass. |
| **Molar volume (gas, 0 °C, 1 atm)** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | Standard molar volume. |
| **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ | Strong covalent bond. |
| **Acidity/basicity** | Acts as a weak acid (forming H⁺) and a strong base (forming H⁻) in superacids or superbases. |
| **Oxidation states** | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride), 0 (molecular). |
| **Reactivity** | Highly reactive with most elements; forms hydrides, acids, and organometallics. |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman, Balmer, Paschen series (UV, visible, IR). | Classic hydrogen spectrum used in astrophysics. |
| **Applications** | Fuel (liquid hydrogen), rocket propellant, hydrogenation reactions, semiconductor doping, medical imaging (MRI contrast agents), fusion research. |

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element**: Only one proton and one electron.
- **Highly reactive**: Forms bonds with almost every element; key in organic chemistry and industrial processes.
- **Low boiling/melting points**: Requires cryogenic handling; liquid hydrogen is a common rocket fuel.
- **Strong ionization energy & electronegativity**: Makes it a powerful oxidizer and a good electron acceptor.
- **Isotopic variants**: Deuterium and tritium are crucial for nuclear fusion and tracer studies.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
